screens.title: Interactive UI Elements: Buttons, Toggles, Sliders, Input Fields
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn the concrete mechanics of Unity's core interactive controls and how to connect them to C# logic. We'll cover buttons that trigger actions, toggles that manage boolean states, sliders for continuous values like volume, and input fields for text entry. You will see both Inspector-based wiring and programmatic listeners using AddListener and RemoveListener, plus initialization patterns to keep UI and game state in sync. This matters because UI is how players control settings and provide input; if events are miswired or not initialized correctly, settings will be out of sync or produce runtime bugs. For example, a StartGame method exposed as a public void can be assigned to a Button's OnClick event in the Inspector, and a Slider's value can be initialized to AudioListener. volume in Start so players don't get a surprise mute. We'll also touch on Toggle Group usage for radio-like choices and basic input validation for names. By the end of this module you'll be able to wire UI both in-editor and in code, avoid common lifecycle pitfalls, and write clear event cleanup to prevent memory or reference errors. Ready to explore each element and a small options-panel walkthrough that ties them together?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Implementation & Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives panel emphasizes the practical patterns you'll apply when building dynamic UI. You will learn to assign UI component references in C# using public fields, serialized private fields, or GetComponent when appropriate, and you will learn when to prefer each method. You will practice using AddListener to attach handlers in Start and RemoveListener in OnDestroy to prevent leaked references when GameObjects are destroyed. You will also adopt a pattern of synchronizing visual state with persistent settings: for example, set a slider. value to AudioListener. volume in Start, and set a toggle. isOn to the inverse of AudioListener. pause so the UI reflects actual audio state. Finally, we cover TextMeshPro input fields, requiring using TMPro namespace and careful handling of On End Edit for saving settings. These practices reduce runtime surprises, improve testability, and make dynamic UIs reliable when scenes change or UI elements are created at runtime. Each objective pairs a small verification task so you can confirm the pattern in a running scene.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Learning Objectives

Implementation & Best Practices

Concrete wiring patterns and lifecycle safety for robust UI event handling.

Reference Assignment
Use public or [SerializeField] fields and drag references in the Inspector to avoid expensive Find calls in Update loops.
Listener Lifecycle
Add listeners in Start, remove them in OnDestroy to prevent dangling callbacks and memory leaks.
State Sync
Always set slider.value and toggle.isOn from current game settings so UI reflects reality when a scene loads.
Key Takeaway
Consistent wiring and listener cleanup keep UI responsive and safe across scene changes.

screens.title: Button Fundamentals and Inspector Wiring
screens.narratorSegment: Buttons are the simplest interactive element but they require precise method signatures to work reliably with the Inspector. A Button component exposes an OnClick() UnityEvent in the Inspector. To connect a method from the Inspector, that method must be public, return void, and take zero parameters or a single parameter of a UnityEvent-compatible type if you intend to pass an argument. A typical example is a MainMenuManager with a public void StartGame() method. You drag the GameObject that has the MainMenuManager script into the OnClick Object slot, and then choose StartGame from the dropdown. That connection causes the method to run when the player clicks the button. A common misconception is that any private or static method can be wired from the Inspector — it cannot. Another misconception is expecting methods with complex parameters to be wired directly; Inspector wiring supports only specific serializable parameter types. For dynamic UIs, AddListener is an alternative: startGameButton. onClick. AddListener(StartGame) attaches the same method in code. When demonstrating, show both the Inspector assignment and the code snippet so you see how the same public void works in both contexts. Example: use a StartGame method that logs and updates status text, then call scene-loading logic from there. Final takeaway: keep public methods small and focused so inspector wiring remains readable, and prefer programmatic listeners for runtime-created buttons.

keyIdea.title: Button wiring rule
keyIdea.text: Inspector requires public void methods with zero or supported single parameter; use AddListener for dynamic attachments.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Button Fundamentals
Core Concept

Inspector OnClick wiring

Connect a GameObject that holds a public void method to the Button's OnClick event in the Inspector. Signature and visibility matter.

Key points
  • Method must be public and return void to appear in the Inspector dropdown.
  • Zero parameters are allowed; one parameter must be a serializable UnityEvent type to pass via Inspector.
  • Use AddListener when creating or modifying buttons at runtime instead of relying on the Inspector.
Common mistake
Trying to wire private or static methods in the Inspector or expecting arbitrary parameter types to work.
Code walkthrough
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.UI;

public class MainMenuManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    public Button startGameButton; // optional if wiring in Inspector

    public void Start()
    {
        if (startGameButton != null)
            startGameButton.onClick.AddListener(StartGame);
    }

    public void StartGame()
    {
        Debug.Log("Game Started!");
        // Load scene or start sequence
    }

    void OnDestroy()
    {
        if (startGameButton != null)
            startGameButton.onClick.RemoveListener(StartGame);
    }
}
Key Takeaway
Inspector wiring is convenient for static UI; programmatic listeners are safer for dynamic interfaces and lifecycle control.

screens.title: Method Signatures and Inspector Constraints
screens.narratorSegment: Inspector-based UnityEvents rely on reflection and a limited set of supported signatures. When you assign a method to a Button's OnClick or a Toggle's On Value Changed in the Inspector, Unity presents only public instance methods that match the expected parameter set. For OnClick, that means methods that return void and take zero parameters, or methods compatible with the event's declared parameter type when a parameter is exposed. For Toggle's On Value Changed(Boolean) you can wire a public void MethodName(bool value) and the toggle will pass the boolean state automatically. A common confusion comes from thinking static methods or private methods will appear — they will not. Another misconception is that any complex type can be passed from the Inspector; only a limited set of types are serializable in the UnityEvent dropdown. Practically, this means design your UI handlers with simple signatures: public void SetMusicEnabled(bool enabled), public void SetVolume(float value), public void OnPlayerNameEntered(string name). This approach keeps inspector wiring straightforward and debuggable. As an example, if you need to call a method with multiple parameters, create a small adapter public void AdapterMethod() that reads fields or properties and then calls the richer method internally. That preserves Inspector convenience while keeping your application logic flexible. Final takeaway: match method signatures to the UI event or use small adapters to bridge gaps.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Method Signatures
Definition

Inspector signature constraints

UI events expose a controlled set of method signatures. Design handler methods to match or adapt to these signatures.

Examples
  • Button.OnClick → public void StartGame()
  • Toggle.OnValueChanged(Boolean) → public void SetMusicEnabled(bool isOn)
  • Slider.OnValueChanged(Single) → public void SetVolume(float value)
  • InputField.OnEndEdit(String) → public void OnPlayerNameEntered(string name)
Misconception
Not all method types are available in the Inspector; static or private methods won't appear.
Adapter pattern

When your game logic needs more arguments or complex state, expose a simple public adapter method for inspector wiring and delegate to richer internal methods.

public void ApplySettings()
{
    // adapter that reads fields and calls complex logic
    ApplySettingsInternal(currentQuality, currentVolume, playerName);
}
Key Takeaway
Keep inspector-exposed methods simple; use adapters to call richer logic within your codebase.

screens.title: Toggle Components and Boolean Events
screens.narratorSegment: A Toggle represents a boolean on/off state and is ideal for settings like enabling music or inverting an axis. Visually, a Toggle has a background and a checkmark image that appears when the toggle is on. Its key runtime hook is On Value Changed(Boolean), which fires with the current boolean value every time the user flips the toggle. To respond, create a public void SetMusicEnabled(bool isEnabled) method and connect it in the Inspector or add a listener in code. A practical example is toggling audio: SetMusicEnabled can set AudioListener. pause =! isEnabled and update a status label. Toggles can be grouped using a Toggle Group component on the parent GameObject to behave like radio buttons—this ensures only one toggle is active at once. A common pitfall is failing to initialize toggle. isOn to match the saved or current game state, causing a mismatch between the UI and behavior. When setting up toggles, decide whether the Inspector wiring or AddListener pattern better fits your flow. For static option screens inspector wiring is simple; for runtime-generated options AddListener provides stability and easier cleanup. Final question to reflect on: when would you prefer Toggle Group over a custom selection script?

keyIdea.title: Toggle tip
keyIdea.text: Use On Value Changed(Boolean) to react to state changes and Toggle Group when only one option should be active.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Toggles
Core Concept

Toggle state and events

Toggles fire On Value Changed(Boolean) with the new state. Use it to toggle game options and keep UI state synchronized.

Practical example
Implement SetMusicEnabled(bool isEnabled) to set AudioListener.pause = !isEnabled and update status text. Initialize toggle.isOn = !AudioListener.pause in Start so visuals match audio state on load.
Common mistake
Not initializing the toggle to match saved game state, causing confusing toggles that don't reflect actual behavior.
Toggle Group quick guide
Add a Toggle Group component to a parent GameObject and assign each Toggle's Group property so only one in the group is active at a time, useful for difficulty settings or mutually exclusive options.
Key Takeaway
Use toggles for booleans and Toggle Group for radio-like choices; always initialize their state from current settings.

screens.title: Setting up a Slider for Continuous Values
screens.narratorSegment: Sliders provide continuous numeric input and are commonly used for audio volume, brightness, or tuning game parameters. When configuring a slider in the Inspector, set Min Value and Max Value to bound the input, and decide whether Whole Numbers should be enabled for discrete steps. The Slider's On Value Changed(Single) event passes a float that you can bind to a public void SetVolume(float value) method. In code you can also subscribe using volumeSlider. onValueChanged. AddListener(SetVolume). Always initialize the slider's value in Start to reflect the current game state, for example volumeSlider. value = AudioListener. volume. A frequent mistake is forgetting to set this value, making the UI out of sync at launch. For UX, consider the mapping between slider range and user perception — 0 to 1 is common for audio, but a 0 to 100 scale may be more readable for players. When using whole numbers, set Min and Max appropriately; for high precision low-range values, keep floating point. Example: use SetVolume to set AudioListener. volume and update a percent label using (value * 100). To avoid noisy updates, if you perform expensive operations on value change, throttle or commit only on EndDrag events in custom handlers. Final takeaway: define clear ranges and initialize the slider so the control always reflects the game state.

keyIdea.text: Set sensible Min/Max, choose whole numbers when appropriate, and initialize value in Start to avoid mismatch with game state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Slider Setup
Process Flow

Configure and initialize Slider

1. Set Min/Max
Choose a range that matches your parameter semantics, e.g., 0 to 1 for audio.
2. Choose Whole Numbers
Enable for discrete steps like levels; keep floats for fine control.
3. Wire OnValueChanged
Bind to a public void SetVolume(float) or add a listener in code.
4. Initialize value in Start
Set slider.value to the current game setting to avoid mismatch.
Concrete example
public void Start()
{
    if (volumeSlider != null)
    {
        volumeSlider.onValueChanged.AddListener(SetVolume);
        volumeSlider.value = AudioListener.volume; // sync at start
    }
}

public void SetVolume(float volume)
{
    AudioListener.volume = volume;
    // update UI percent label: (volume * 100).ToString("F0") + "%"
}
Key Takeaway
Sliders must be initialized and have appropriate ranges; decide precision based on UX expectations.

screens.title: Input Fields: Text Entry, Events, and Validation
screens.narratorSegment: Input Fields are the primary way to collect text from players, for example a player name for a leaderboard. TextMeshPro Input Fields add better typography and require the TMPro namespace in C#. They expose On Value Changed(String), which fires on every text change and is useful for real-time validation, and On End Edit(String), which fires when the user commits their entry. Use On Value Changed to filter characters or display immediate feedback, and use On End Edit to persist a final value to PlayerPrefs or to trigger a submission. Input fields include Inspector options like Character Limit, Content Type (Alphanumeric, Integer, Password), and Line Type. For sensitive entries, set Content Type to Password to mask input. A common error is trusting Inspector validation alone; for strict rules like letters and spaces only you should implement C# validation, for example checking char. IsLetter() or char. IsWhiteSpace() and removing invalid characters in On Value Changed. Also initialize playerNameInputField. text in Start to load a saved name so the UI reflects stored settings. This keeps a predictable experience and reduces surprises when the scene begins. Final thought: balance real-time filtering with user freedom; aggressive filtering can feel intrusive unless clearly communicated.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Input Fields
Definition

Text entry and events

Use On Value Changed(String) for live feedback and On End Edit(String) for final submission or saving.

Inspector options
  • Character Limit — prevent overly long names
  • Content Type — choose Password, Alphanumeric, Integer when appropriate
  • Line Type — Single Line for names, Multi Line for chat
Validation example
public void ValidatePlayerName(string currentText)
{
    string validated = "";
    foreach (char c in currentText)
    {
        if (char.IsLetter(c) || char.IsWhiteSpace(c)) validated += c;
    }
    if (playerNameInputField.text != validated)
        playerNameInputField.text = validated; // enforce letters and spaces only
}
Key Takeaway
Do not rely on Inspector alone for strict validation — implement checks in code and initialize saved text in Start.

screens.title: Programmatic Listeners: AddListener & RemoveListener
screens.narratorSegment: Programmatic listeners give you precise control for dynamic UIs and are essential when UI elements are created or destroyed at runtime. The pattern is straightforward: in Start attach callbacks using AddListener, and in OnDestroy remove them using RemoveListener. This prevents dangling callbacks that can call into destroyed objects and cause exceptions or memory leaks. For example, in UIManager Start you might add startGameButton. onClick. AddListener(StartGame), musicToggle. onValueChanged. AddListener(SetMusicEnabled), volumeSlider. onValueChanged. AddListener(SetVolume), and playerNameInputField. onEndEdit. AddListener(OnPlayerNameEntered). In OnDestroy reverse this by calling RemoveListener with the same method references. A subtle but common pitfall is using anonymous delegates when you later attempt to remove them — RemoveListener requires the same delegate instance, so named methods are easier to remove. Another important detail is to guard null checks in Start so the code remains robust if fields were not assigned. Choosing programmatic listeners also helps when adding behaviors dynamically to prefabs; you can subscribe immediately after instantiating. A concrete example: initialize UI values from PlayerPrefs then subscribe to events. This sequence ensures the UI reflects current state immediately and that subscribed handlers won't run during initialization unless explicitly intended. Final takeaway: add in Start, remove in OnDestroy, and prefer named handlers for reliable cleanup.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Programmatic Listeners
Process Flow

Attach in Start, remove in OnDestroy

This pattern prevents callbacks from firing against destroyed targets and keeps memory clean when UI elements are dynamic.

  • Guard nulls: if (toggle != null) toggle.onValueChanged.AddListener(SetMusicEnabled);
  • Remove listeners using the same method references in OnDestroy.
  • Avoid anonymous delegates if you need to remove listeners later.
Example
void Start()
{
    if (musicToggle != null)
    {
        musicToggle.onValueChanged.AddListener(SetMusicEnabled);
        musicToggle.isOn = !AudioListener.pause;
    }
}

void OnDestroy()
{
    if (musicToggle != null)
        musicToggle.onValueChanged.RemoveListener(SetMusicEnabled);
}
Common mistake
Adding listeners without removing them, or using anonymous delegates which cannot be reliably removed later.

screens.title: Inspector Wiring vs Programmatic Listeners
screens.narratorSegment: There are two common ways to connect UI and logic in Unity: Inspector wiring and programmatic listeners. Inspector wiring is quick and visible in the Editor: you drag a GameObject into an event slot and pick a public method. This is excellent for static UI that doesn't change at runtime and for designers who prefer a visual mapping. The downside is less control over lifecycle and difficulty when UI is dynamically instantiated. Programmatic listeners via AddListener give you explicit control: you can attach handlers at runtime, choose timing, and easily remove listeners in OnDestroy for safe cleanup. This is better for dynamic menus, spawned UI, or when you need to change behavior conditionally. A misconception is that Inspector wiring is inherently unsafe — it is safe for static components but becomes brittle if elements are created or destroyed at runtime. A practical hybrid approach is to use inspector wiring for stable root UI and AddListener for runtime-generated elements or when wiring must happen based on game state. Example: static main menu buttons assigned in the Inspector, while options generated per player choice are subscribed in code. Final takeaway: pick Inspector for stable, declarative wiring and AddListener when you need programmatic control and robust lifecycle management.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Inspector vs Programmatic
Inspector Wiring
  • Easy visual mapping for static UI and designer workflows.
  • Requires public void method signatures.
  • Less flexible for runtime-generated elements.
Programmatic Listeners
  • AddListener/RemoveListener gives precise lifecycle control.
  • Essential for dynamic menus, prefab instantiation, and conditional behavior.
  • Prefer named handlers to ensure RemoveListener works correctly.
Hybrid recommendation
Use Inspector wiring for stable root UI and AddListener for elements created or modified at runtime. This balances clarity and control.

screens.title: UIManager Example: Wiring a Simple Options Panel
screens.narratorSegment: The UIManager pattern centralizes UI references and event handling for a small options panel. In the chapter example, UIManager holds public fields for a start button, a music toggle, a volume slider, a TextMeshPro input field, and a status text. In Start it assigns listeners and initializes control values from AudioListener and PlayerPrefs. It also demonstrates OnDestroy cleanup to remove listeners. This architecture makes the panel easy to debug because all wiring is in one place, and it offers an obvious spot to persist user choices. A concrete walkthrough: set musicToggle. isOn =! AudioListener. pause, set volumeSlider. value = AudioListener. volume, and set playerNameInputField. text = PlayerPrefs. GetString("PlayerName","New Player"). Then add listeners that call SetMusicEnabled, SetVolume, and OnPlayerNameEntered. In OnPlayerNameEntered you validate the input, save with PlayerPrefs. SetString and update the status text. A common oversight is forgetting to include using TMPro; without it TMP_InputField references won't compile. The final takeaway: a centralized UIManager improves maintainability and makes initialization and cleanup predictable. Consider splitting responsibilities if the UI grows larger, but this pattern works well for compact panels. keyIdea.text: Centralize UI references and lifecycle wiring in one manager for small panels; initialize values and clean up listeners consistently.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › UIManager Example

Options Panel Architecture

Group related UI elements and handlers under a single manager for small panels so initialization and cleanup happen together.

  • Declare public fields for each UI component and assign in the Inspector.
  • Initialize control values from AudioListener and PlayerPrefs in Start.
  • Subscribe to events with AddListener and unsubscribe in OnDestroy.
Canonical snippet
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.UI;
using TMPro;

public class UIManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    public Toggle musicToggle;
    public Slider volumeSlider;
    public TMP_InputField playerNameInputField;

    void Start()
    {
        if (musicToggle != null)
        {
            musicToggle.onValueChanged.AddListener(SetMusicEnabled);
            musicToggle.isOn = !AudioListener.pause;
        }
        if (volumeSlider != null)
        {
            volumeSlider.onValueChanged.AddListener(SetVolume);
            volumeSlider.value = AudioListener.volume;
        }
        if (playerNameInputField != null)
        {
            playerNameInputField.onEndEdit.AddListener(OnPlayerNameEntered);
            playerNameInputField.text = PlayerPrefs.GetString("PlayerName", "New Player");
        }
    }

    // ... handlers and cleanup ...
}
Key Takeaway
A single manager simplifies wiring and debugging for compact UI panels; split responsibilities as a panel grows.

screens.title: Validation, Security, and UX Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Validating user input is both a UX and a security concern. For player names, you'll often want to restrict characters, enforce a length, and sanitize input before saving or sending it to a server. Unity's Input Field Inspector settings help, but they are not a substitute for code validation. Implement On Value Changed-based filtering to remove disallowed characters in real time or show an inline error message. Example validation logic checks each character with char. IsLetter or char. IsWhiteSpace and constructs a validated string; if the field's text differs, update it to the cleaned value and show a warning. Also enforce a Character Limit and trim whitespace at the edges when saving. For passwords or other sensitive fields, use the Password content type to mask entries. A common misunderstanding is to rely on client-side validation alone; always validate again on the server. In the context of single-player games, validation still improves the player's experience and prevents UI-breaking characters. Another UX concern is default values: choose sensible defaults and ensure saved settings are loaded in Start so the UI never surprises the player. Final takeaway: validate input, set sensible defaults, and persist thoughtfully so players see consistent, safe results.

keyIdea.text: Filter and sanitize input in code, do not rely solely on Inspector options, and load sensible defaults at startup.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Validation & UX

Validation Patterns

Filter and sanitize input to avoid invalid characters, enforce length, and present helpful feedback to players.

  • Use On Value Changed to remove invalid characters in real time for names.
  • Trim and validate again on On End Edit before saving to PlayerPrefs.
  • For sensitive data, use Password content type and treat it carefully in code.
Example rule
public void OnPlayerNameEntered(string name)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name)) name = "Guest";
    PlayerPrefs.SetString("PlayerName", name);
}
UX tip
Provide clear error messages or auto-correction to help players fix invalid input rather than silently changing it.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: We covered the core Unity UI elements and practical wiring patterns: Buttons trigger public void methods via OnClick or AddListener; Toggles fire On Value Changed with a boolean and use Toggle Group for exclusive options; Sliders deliver continuous float values and must be initialized to match game state; Input Fields offer live and commit events and require validation and the TMPro namespace when using TextMeshPro. You learned programmatic listener patterns—AddListener in Start and RemoveListener in OnDestroy—for robust lifecycle control and when to prefer Inspector wiring versus programmatic wiring. The hands-on options panel ties these ideas together: initialize UI from AudioListener and PlayerPrefs, respond to user changes, validate input, and persist preferences. Remember the common pitfalls: incorrect method signatures for Inspector wiring, failing to initialize sliders and toggles, not removing listeners, and trusting Inspector settings alone for validation. Use the UIManager pattern for compact panels and split responsibilities when complexity grows. Ask yourself: does each UI control reflect the current game state on scene start, and are listeners cleaned up when no longer needed? That check will prevent many bugs.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Key Concepts
Button
Triggers public void methods through OnClick or AddListener for dynamic UI.
Toggle
Represents a boolean; use Toggle Group for exclusive selections.
Slider
Continuous input; set range and initialize value from game settings.
Input Field
Use On Value Changed for live validation and On End Edit for commits; validate in code.
AddListener / RemoveListener

Validation & Init

Final takeaway

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three compact rules in mind as you implement interactive UI: first, match method signatures for Inspector wiring or use programmatic listeners when you need dynamic control. Second, always initialize UI controls from the current game state so visuals and behavior align; sliders and toggles are frequent causes of mismatch when not set at Start. Third, validate inputs in code and remove listeners in OnDestroy to avoid runtime surprises and memory leaks. These three practices address the majority of bugs you will encounter while building options panels and small menus. If you follow them you'll produce UI that behaves predictably for players and is easier to maintain for developers. What to Remember means signature compatibility, initialization from state, and lifecycle-safe listeners are the foundations of reliable ui.. In practical terms, three compact concepts to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Signature compatibility, initialization from state, and lifecycle-safe listeners are the foundations of reliable UI.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What to Remember
Signatures
Use public void and supported parameter types for Inspector wiring; otherwise use AddListener.
Initialize
Set toggle.isOn and slider.value from AudioListener and saved settings in Start.
Lifecycle
Add listeners in Start, remove in OnDestroy, and validate input in code before saving.
Closing thought
These small, consistent practices drastically reduce bugs and improve the player's experience with your game settings UI.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn the concrete mechanics of Unity's core interactive controls and how to connect them to C# logic. We'll cover buttons that trigger actions, toggles that manage boolean states, sliders for continuous values like volume, and input fields for text entry. You will see both Inspector-based wiring and programmatic listeners using AddListener and RemoveListener, plus initialization patterns to keep UI and game state in sync. This matters because UI is how players control settings and provide input; if events are miswired or not initialized correctly, settings will be out of sync or produce runtime bugs. For example, a StartGame method exposed as a public void can be assigned to a Button's OnClick event in the Inspector, and a Slider's value can be initialized to AudioListener. volume in Start so players don't get a surprise mute. We'll also touch on Toggle Group usage for radio-like choices and basic input validation for names. By the end of this module you'll be able to wire UI both in-editor and in code, avoid common lifecycle pitfalls, and write clear event cleanup to prevent memory or reference errors. Ready to explore each element and a small options-panel walkthrough that ties them together?

By the end of this chapter you will implement Unity Button components to trigger C# methods and understand the public method constraints required by Inspector wiring. You'll configure Toggle components and Toggle Groups to manage boolean states, and you'll connect their events to functions that accept a boolean parameter. You'll set up Sliders for continuous values like audio, initialize them from game state, and handle common mistakes such as failing to set the initial value. You'll also create TMP Input Fields for player names, wire On Value Changed and On End Edit events, and implement simple validation to accept only letters and spaces. Each objective includes hands-on wiring and at least one C# pattern: Inspector assignment, AddListener/RemoveListener usage, and lifecycle cleanup in OnDestroy. These skills matter because UI is the bridge between the player's intent and game behavior; when events are organized and initialized correctly the user experience becomes predictable and robust. Expect practical examples that show both the Inspector method connection and programmatic listener setup so you can choose the right approach for static or dynamic UI.

This second objectives panel emphasizes the practical patterns you'll apply when building dynamic UI. You will learn to assign UI component references in C# using public fields, serialized private fields, or GetComponent when appropriate, and you will learn when to prefer each method. You will practice using AddListener to attach handlers in Start and RemoveListener in OnDestroy to prevent leaked references when GameObjects are destroyed. You will also adopt a pattern of synchronizing visual state with persistent settings: for example, set a slider. value to AudioListener. volume in Start, and set a toggle. isOn to the inverse of AudioListener. pause so the UI reflects actual audio state. Finally, we cover TextMeshPro input fields, requiring using TMPro namespace and careful handling of On End Edit for saving settings. These practices reduce runtime surprises, improve testability, and make dynamic UIs reliable when scenes change or UI elements are created at runtime. Each objective pairs a small verification task so you can confirm the pattern in a running scene.

Buttons are the simplest interactive element but they require precise method signatures to work reliably with the Inspector. A Button component exposes an OnClick() UnityEvent in the Inspector. To connect a method from the Inspector, that method must be public, return void, and take zero parameters or a single parameter of a UnityEvent-compatible type if you intend to pass an argument. A typical example is a MainMenuManager with a public void StartGame() method. You drag the GameObject that has the MainMenuManager script into the OnClick Object slot, and then choose StartGame from the dropdown. That connection causes the method to run when the player clicks the button. A common misconception is that any private or static method can be wired from the Inspector — it cannot. Another misconception is expecting methods with complex parameters to be wired directly; Inspector wiring supports only specific serializable parameter types. For dynamic UIs, AddListener is an alternative: startGameButton. onClick. AddListener(StartGame) attaches the same method in code. When demonstrating, show both the Inspector assignment and the code snippet so you see how the same public void works in both contexts. Example: use a StartGame method that logs and updates status text, then call scene-loading logic from there. Final takeaway: keep public methods small and focused so inspector wiring remains readable, and prefer programmatic listeners for runtime-created buttons.

Inspector-based UnityEvents rely on reflection and a limited set of supported signatures. When you assign a method to a Button's OnClick or a Toggle's On Value Changed in the Inspector, Unity presents only public instance methods that match the expected parameter set. For OnClick, that means methods that return void and take zero parameters, or methods compatible with the event's declared parameter type when a parameter is exposed. For Toggle's On Value Changed(Boolean) you can wire a public void MethodName(bool value) and the toggle will pass the boolean state automatically. A common confusion comes from thinking static methods or private methods will appear — they will not. Another misconception is that any complex type can be passed from the Inspector; only a limited set of types are serializable in the UnityEvent dropdown. Practically, this means design your UI handlers with simple signatures: public void SetMusicEnabled(bool enabled), public void SetVolume(float value), public void OnPlayerNameEntered(string name). This approach keeps inspector wiring straightforward and debuggable. As an example, if you need to call a method with multiple parameters, create a small adapter public void AdapterMethod() that reads fields or properties and then calls the richer method internally. That preserves Inspector convenience while keeping your application logic flexible. Final takeaway: match method signatures to the UI event or use small adapters to bridge gaps.

A Toggle represents a boolean on/off state and is ideal for settings like enabling music or inverting an axis. Visually, a Toggle has a background and a checkmark image that appears when the toggle is on. Its key runtime hook is On Value Changed(Boolean), which fires with the current boolean value every time the user flips the toggle. To respond, create a public void SetMusicEnabled(bool isEnabled) method and connect it in the Inspector or add a listener in code. A practical example is toggling audio: SetMusicEnabled can set AudioListener. pause =! isEnabled and update a status label. Toggles can be grouped using a Toggle Group component on the parent GameObject to behave like radio buttons—this ensures only one toggle is active at once. A common pitfall is failing to initialize toggle. isOn to match the saved or current game state, causing a mismatch between the UI and behavior. When setting up toggles, decide whether the Inspector wiring or AddListener pattern better fits your flow. For static option screens inspector wiring is simple; for runtime-generated options AddListener provides stability and easier cleanup. Final question to reflect on: when would you prefer Toggle Group over a custom selection script?

Sliders provide continuous numeric input and are commonly used for audio volume, brightness, or tuning game parameters. When configuring a slider in the Inspector, set Min Value and Max Value to bound the input, and decide whether Whole Numbers should be enabled for discrete steps. The Slider's On Value Changed(Single) event passes a float that you can bind to a public void SetVolume(float value) method. In code you can also subscribe using volumeSlider. onValueChanged. AddListener(SetVolume). Always initialize the slider's value in Start to reflect the current game state, for example volumeSlider. value = AudioListener. volume. A frequent mistake is forgetting to set this value, making the UI out of sync at launch. For UX, consider the mapping between slider range and user perception — 0 to 1 is common for audio, but a 0 to 100 scale may be more readable for players. When using whole numbers, set Min and Max appropriately; for high precision low-range values, keep floating point. Example: use SetVolume to set AudioListener. volume and update a percent label using (value * 100). To avoid noisy updates, if you perform expensive operations on value change, throttle or commit only on EndDrag events in custom handlers. Final takeaway: define clear ranges and initialize the slider so the control always reflects the game state.

Input Fields are the primary way to collect text from players, for example a player name for a leaderboard. TextMeshPro Input Fields add better typography and require the TMPro namespace in C#. They expose On Value Changed(String), which fires on every text change and is useful for real-time validation, and On End Edit(String), which fires when the user commits their entry. Use On Value Changed to filter characters or display immediate feedback, and use On End Edit to persist a final value to PlayerPrefs or to trigger a submission. Input fields include Inspector options like Character Limit, Content Type (Alphanumeric, Integer, Password), and Line Type. For sensitive entries, set Content Type to Password to mask input. A common error is trusting Inspector validation alone; for strict rules like letters and spaces only you should implement C# validation, for example checking char. IsLetter() or char. IsWhiteSpace() and removing invalid characters in On Value Changed. Also initialize playerNameInputField. text in Start to load a saved name so the UI reflects stored settings. This keeps a predictable experience and reduces surprises when the scene begins. Final thought: balance real-time filtering with user freedom; aggressive filtering can feel intrusive unless clearly communicated.

Programmatic listeners give you precise control for dynamic UIs and are essential when UI elements are created or destroyed at runtime. The pattern is straightforward: in Start attach callbacks using AddListener, and in OnDestroy remove them using RemoveListener. This prevents dangling callbacks that can call into destroyed objects and cause exceptions or memory leaks. For example, in UIManager Start you might add startGameButton. onClick. AddListener(StartGame), musicToggle. onValueChanged. AddListener(SetMusicEnabled), volumeSlider. onValueChanged. AddListener(SetVolume), and playerNameInputField. onEndEdit. AddListener(OnPlayerNameEntered). In OnDestroy reverse this by calling RemoveListener with the same method references. A subtle but common pitfall is using anonymous delegates when you later attempt to remove them — RemoveListener requires the same delegate instance, so named methods are easier to remove. Another important detail is to guard null checks in Start so the code remains robust if fields were not assigned. Choosing programmatic listeners also helps when adding behaviors dynamically to prefabs; you can subscribe immediately after instantiating. A concrete example: initialize UI values from PlayerPrefs then subscribe to events. This sequence ensures the UI reflects current state immediately and that subscribed handlers won't run during initialization unless explicitly intended. Final takeaway: add in Start, remove in OnDestroy, and prefer named handlers for reliable cleanup.

Final takeaway: pick Inspector for stable, declarative wiring and AddListener when you need programmatic control and robust lifecycle management.

Validating user input is both a UX and a security concern. For player names, you'll often want to restrict characters, enforce a length, and sanitize input before saving or sending it to a server. Unity's Input Field Inspector settings help, but they are not a substitute for code validation. Implement On Value Changed-based filtering to remove disallowed characters in real time or show an inline error message. Example validation logic checks each character with char. IsLetter or char. IsWhiteSpace and constructs a validated string; if the field's text differs, update it to the cleaned value and show a warning. Also enforce a Character Limit and trim whitespace at the edges when saving. For passwords or other sensitive fields, use the Password content type to mask entries. A common misunderstanding is to rely on client-side validation alone; always validate again on the server. In the context of single-player games, validation still improves the player's experience and prevents UI-breaking characters. Another UX concern is default values: choose sensible defaults and ensure saved settings are loaded in Start so the UI never surprises the player. Keep three compact rules in mind as you implement interactive UI: first, match method signatures for Inspector wiring or use programmatic listeners when you need dynamic control. Second, always initialize UI controls from the current game state so visuals and behavior align; sliders and toggles are frequent causes of mismatch when not set at Start. Third, validate inputs in code and remove listeners in OnDestroy to avoid runtime surprises and memory leaks.
